## 1. The question

The project asks how much statistics can catch without predefined signatures, and how often it gets
it wrong. This chapter measures the errors, and how sure we can be of those measurements. It
compares three detectors on the same requests:

- **rules**: signatures only. A request is flagged when a regular expression matches.
- **stats**: statistics only. A request is flagged when its anomaly score `s = −log10 p`, learned
  from legitimate traffic, reaches a threshold.
- **combined**: a request is flagged on a rule match, or when the score reaches the threshold.

## 2. Experimental design

Each **seed** draws a complete dataset from the traffic generator (T4, ADR-006), in three splits:

| Split       | Requests | Content                                           | Used for                      |
| ----------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| train       | 2,000    | legitimate only                                   | fitting the statistical model |
| calibration | 10,000   | legitimate only                                   | choosing the threshold        |
| test        | 5,000    | 4,500 legitimate (225 hard cases) and 500 attacks | measuring the errors, once    |

- **Labels never reach the model or the threshold.** The model is fitted on legitimate requests only
  (ADR-004), and the threshold is chosen on legitimate requests only (ADR-009). Attack labels are
  used once, to score the test split. Choosing the threshold that looks best on the test set would
  inflate every number.
- **Attacks** are legitimate requests with one value replaced by a payload. They come in three
  variants:
  - canonical: known signatures;
  - obfuscated: disguised to dodge the signatures;
  - novel: families the rules have no signature for.

  Five of the nine families are novel, so novel attacks are more than half of the attacks: 258-296
  of the 500 in each seed.

- **Hard cases** are legitimate requests that look odd: an apostrophe, long free text, non-Latin
  text. They are only in the test split, so they show how the detector handles traffic the
  calibration never saw.
- **20 seeds** give 20 independent replications of the whole procedure: new data, new model, new
  thresholds.

## 3. Methods

### 3.1 Error rates, not accuracy

From the confusion matrix (TP, FN, FP, TN) the chapter reports:

- the true-positive rate, `TPR = TP / (TP + FN)` (recall), and its complement the false-negative
  rate, `FNR = 1 − TPR`;
- the false-positive rate, `FPR = FP / (FP + TN)`;
- the precision, `TP / (TP + FP)`.

Accuracy is not reported. With 90% legitimate requests, a detector that never raises an alert would
score 90%.

### 3.2 A threshold for a target false-positive rate

Take the scores of `n` legitimate calibration requests and a target `α`. At most `k = ⌊α·n⌋` of them
may reach the threshold. The threshold `t` is the smallest number strictly above the `(k+1)`-th
largest score: an empirical quantile of the legitimate scores (`thresholdAtFpr`).

- **Ties** move together, so the calibration FPR can fall below `α`.
- **Size:** the quantile rests on the `k` largest scores, and with fewer than about 10 of them it is
  noisy. So the calibration split has 10,000 requests: `n ≥ 10/α` even at `α = 0.1%`.
- **An unattainable target:** in combined mode a rule match scores `+∞` and is flagged at any
  threshold. If more than `k` legitimate calibration requests match a rule, no threshold meets the
  target. The threshold then sits above every finite calibration score, and only the rules fire on
  the calibration split. This happened with the baseline ruleset (§5).

Kruegel and Vigna (2003) likewise set their thresholds on attack-free traffic.

### 3.3 ROC curve and AUC

The ROC curve sweeps the threshold down through every distinct score and plots TPR against FPR. The
area under it is the Mann-Whitney statistic:

```
AUC = P(score of a random attack > score of a random legitimate request), ties counting ½
```

0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect separation. The AUC uses only the ranking of the scores, so it does
not depend on any threshold. The rules have a binary score: their curve has a single inner point,
and `AUC = (1 + TPR − FPR) / 2`.

### 3.4 Uncertainty within one run

Every rate is a proportion `x/n` estimated from a finite test set. It gets a 95% **Wilson**
interval, with `p̂ = x/n` and `z = 1.96`:

```
centre     = (p̂ + z²/(2n)) / (1 + z²/n)
half-width = z / (1 + z²/n) · √( p̂(1 − p̂)/n + z²/(4n²) )
```

The textbook Wald interval, `p̂ ± z·√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n)`, collapses to [0, 0] when there are no errors.
Wilson does not: 0 false positives out of 900 gives an FPR in [0, 0.43%], not "zero".

The AUC is not a simple proportion, so it gets a **stratified percentile bootstrap**:

1. resample the attacks and the legitimate requests separately, with replacement, 1,000 times;
2. compute the AUC of each resample;
3. take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

The random numbers come from a generator seeded with the dataset seed + 2³¹. That stream never
overlaps the dataset's, so the intervals are reproducible.

### 3.5 Uncertainty across runs

The intervals of §3.4 describe one test set. Across the 20 seeds everything changes at once:
training data, model, threshold and test set. Each metric is therefore summarised by its mean, its
standard deviation, its range, and a 95% Student-t interval for the mean:

```
mean ± t(0.975, 19) · SD / √20,     t(0.975, 19) = 2.093
```

The seed is the independent unit. The requests of one seed share one model and one threshold, so
they are not independent trials. A Wilson interval on the counts added up over all seeds would
ignore how much the threshold moves from run to run, and come out too narrow.

Sometimes a value is the same in every seed, for example 100% of command-injection attacks caught by
the rules. The interval then has zero width, and the tables say "every seed" instead.

### 3.6 Comparing two detectors on the same requests

The three detectors score the same requests, so their results are paired. **McNemar's test** uses
only the requests where two detectors disagree: `b` flagged by A only, `c` flagged by B only. If the
two were equally good, each disagreement would be a coin flip: `b ~ Binomial(b + c, ½)`.

- The exact two-sided p-value is `2·P(X ≤ min(b, c))`. The textbook χ² with continuity correction,
  `(|b − c| − 1)² / (b + c)`, agrees with it for large counts.
- Attacks, novel attacks and legitimate requests are tested separately. On attacks, flagging more is
  better; on legitimate requests, it means more false alarms. One test on all requests would compare
  accuracy.
- Over the seeds the counts are added up: under the null hypothesis each seed's `b` is binomial, and
  so is the sum.
- There are 18 tests (3 pairs × 3 groups × 2 targets). With a Bonferroni correction, a difference
  counts at p < 0.05/18 ≈ 0.0028.

## 4. Results

All values are the mean over 20 seeds, with the 95% t-interval of the mean in brackets.

### 4.1 Without a threshold: AUC

**Table 1 - AUC on the test split.**

| Detector | AUC                 | SD across seeds | Range       | Mean width of one seed's bootstrap interval |
| -------- | ------------------- | --------------- | ----------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| rules    | 0.704 [0.700-0.709] | 0.010           | 0.687-0.727 | 0.043                                       |
| stats    | 0.993 [0.992-0.993] | 0.001           | 0.992-0.994 | 0.004                                       |
| combined | 0.996 [0.996-0.997] | 0.000           | 0.995-0.997 | 0.002                                       |

On ranking alone, the combination separates attacks from legitimate requests best, and the
statistics clearly beat the rules.

### 4.2 At a 1% false-positive target

**Table 2 - Operating point at a 1% target.**

| Detector | Threshold              | Calibration FPR   | Test FPR, typical | Test FPR, all legitimate | TPR               | Precision         | Target met  |
| -------- | ---------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------ | ----------------- | ----------------- | ----------- |
| rules    | - (a rule match)       | 0% (every seed)   | 0% (every seed)   | 0% (every seed)          | 40.9% [39.9-41.8] | 100% (every seed) | 20/20 seeds |
| stats    | 22.464 [20.899-24.029] | 0.99% [0.98-1.00] | 0.94% [0.84-1.03] | 2.12% [2.01-2.23]        | 91.5% [90.3-92.7] | 82.8% [82.1-83.5] | 20/20       |
| combined | 22.464 [20.899-24.029] | 0.99% [0.98-1.00] | 0.94% [0.84-1.03] | 2.12% [2.01-2.23]        | 96.3% [95.6-97.0] | 83.5% [82.8-84.2] | 20/20       |

The rules flag no legitimate request, so the combination keeps the statistics' threshold: the two
raise the same false alarms, and the combination adds the rule matches.

**Table 3 - Share flagged by variant at a 1% target.** For attacks this is the detection rate; for
legitimate requests, the false-positive rate.

| Variant              | Requests per seed | rules             | stats             | combined          |
| -------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- |
| attack · canonical   | 163-197           | 100% (every seed) | 86.5% [84.7-88.4] | 100% (every seed) |
| attack · obfuscated  | 33-56             | 58.2% [54.8-61.6] | 97.0% [95.8-98.2] | 97.5% [96.3-98.7] |
| attack · novel       | 258-296           | 0% (every seed)   | 93.7% [92.5-95.0] | 93.7% [92.5-95.0] |
| legitimate · typical | 4,275             | 0% (every seed)   | 0.94% [0.84-1.03] | 0.94% [0.84-1.03] |
| legitimate · hard    | 225               | 0% (every seed)   | 24.6% [23.6-25.7] | 24.6% [23.6-25.7] |

By family:

- **The rules** catch every command-injection attack (100% in every seed), and most SQL injection
  (90.9%), XSS (89.4%) and traversal (86.4%). They catch no novel attack at all. They were written
  for the canonical payloads only, without looking at the obfuscated and novel ones (ADR-006, B-01):
  every canonical attack is caught, but only 58% of the obfuscated ones.
- **The statistics** catch between 77% (CRLF injection) and 100% (LDAP injection) of every family.
- **Legitimate requests:** the rules raise no false alarm, 0 of 90,000 legitimate test requests over
  the 20 seeds. Most of the statistics' false alarms (64%) come from `/profile` requests, 12.7% of
  which raise one; `/login` and `/products` requests never raise one.

### 4.3 At a 0.1% false-positive target

All three detectors meet this target.

- **Statistics:** threshold 58.722 [53.099-64.345]; calibration FPR 0.08% [0.07-0.09], test FPR
  1.32% [1.26-1.38]; TPR down to 77.7% [76.5-78.9], precision up to 86.8% [86.3-87.2]; 80.7%
  [79.0-82.4] of novel attacks caught, and no hard case flagged. **[To rewrite: the numbers no
  longer support this sentence (claim loNoHard).]**
- **Combined:** the same threshold and the same false alarms; TPR 88.6% [87.6-89.7], precision 88.2%
  [87.8-88.6].
- **Rules:** no threshold, so the same row as at 1%: no false alarm, TPR 40.9%.

### 4.4 Paired comparisons

**Table 4 - McNemar at a 1% target**, disagreements added up over the 20 seeds.

| A vs B            | Requests      | Flagged only by A | Flagged only by B | Exact p | Seeds with p < 0.05     |
| ----------------- | ------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- | ------- | ----------------------- |
| stats vs combined | attacks       | 0                 | 485               | < 0.001 | combined ahead in 20    |
| stats vs combined | novel attacks | 0                 | 0                 | 1.000   | none                    |
| stats vs combined | legitimate    | 0                 | 0                 | 1.000   | none                    |
| rules vs stats    | attacks       | 485               | 5,544             | < 0.001 | stats ahead in 20       |
| rules vs stats    | novel attacks | 0                 | 5,193             | < 0.001 | stats ahead in 20       |
| rules vs stats    | legitimate    | 0                 | 1,909             | < 0.001 | stats more alarms in 20 |

The statistics and the combination raise exactly the same 1,909 false alarms and catch the same
novel attacks: they never disagree there. The combination adds 485 attacks that the statistics miss,
all canonical or obfuscated, the ones the rules are written for. The rules and the statistics miss
different attacks (485 against 5,544), which is why combining them pays.

At 0.1% the picture is the same: the combination adds 1,094 attacks to the statistics, with the same
1,187 false alarms.

### 4.5 How much do the numbers move?

- **Rules:** the SD of the AUC across seeds (0.010) matches the standard error from one seed's
  bootstrap (≈ 0.043 / 3.92 = 0.011). The rules learn nothing from data, so the only noise is the
  test set.
- **Statistics:** the SD across seeds (0.001) is close to the bootstrap's standard error too (≈
  0.001): one test set accounts for most of the spread, and the training data add little to it. It
  was not so in the first draft. On the raw length (commit `0ca4847`) the SD was 0.028 against
  0.013, and the training data made up about four fifths of the variance. The log scale of C-04 made
  the model far steadier from one training set to the next.
- **The test FPR over all legitimate requests** also moves a lot: SD 0.24%, from 1.67% to 2.60%.
  **[To rewrite: the numbers no longer support this sentence (claim fprMoves).]** How many of the
  four hard-case fixtures fall above the threshold changes from seed to seed.

This is why the experiment uses 20 seeds rather than one.

## 5. Discussion

1. **Calibration works where it has seen data.** On typical legitimate traffic, the statistics keep
   to the targets out of sample: 0.94% [0.84-1.03] against 1%, and 0.09% against 0.1%.
2. **It does not cover what it has not seen.** About one hard case in four (25%) raises a false
   alarm at the 1% target. Neither the calibration split nor the training split holds such requests:
   a model of "normal" is only as wide as the normal traffic it was given.
3. **Statistics catch what signatures cannot.** At 1% they catch 94% of novel attacks, against 0%
   for the rules: this is the core answer to the research question. But they also miss 13% of the
   canonical attacks the rules catch (87% against 100%). So they complement the rules rather than
   replace them.
4. **Combining is free, as long as the rules raise no false alarm.** The signatures of B-01 flag no
   legitimate request, so the combination keeps the statistics' threshold and their false alarms,
   and adds the rule matches: at the 1% target its TPR rises from 91% to 96% with the same 2.12% of
   false positives (McNemar: 485 attacks against 0, in all 20 seeds).
   - The baseline ruleset of the first draft (commit `c4ef25c`, with the raw length signal of the
     time) showed the opposite. It matched 20.6% of the login requests, whose generated passwords
     contain `#` and `--`, so the rules alone flagged 3.1% of legitimate traffic. The combination
     could then never meet a 1% target: its threshold rose from 1.38, the statistics' own, to 2.30,
     and it caught fewer novel attacks than the statistics alone (42% against 59%, McNemar p <
     0.001).
   - The lesson: with a fixed false-positive budget, every false alarm of a rule is paid for by the
     statistics. A signature has to be checked on legitimate traffic before it joins the
     combination.

5. **The base rate changes everything** (T4's chapter). At the 10% prevalence of the test split,
   about 83% of the statistics' alarms are attacks, and 83% of the combination's. At a prevalence
   `π` of 0.1%, Bayes gives:

   ```
   PPV = TPR·π / (TPR·π + FPR·(1 − π))
   ```

   - at the 1% target: 4.1% for the statistics and 4.3% for the combination, so even for the
     combination about 96 alarms in 100 are false;
   - at the 0.1% target: 5.6% and 6.3%.

## 6. Limitations

- **Synthetic data.** The numbers describe the T4 generator, not real traffic. The conclusions that
  carry over are comparative: rules against statistics, what the combination adds and what a rule's
  false alarms cost it, calibration against unseen requests.
- **A baseline model.** The score is still the length signal alone, on the log scale (C-04). **[To
  rewrite: the numbers no longer support this sentence (claim lengthOnly).]** Chi-square (C-03) and
  the outlier signals (C-05) are implemented but enter the score only with C-06: they will change
  every number in Tables 1-4, and `npm run report -- --update` will write the new ones.
- **Four hard cases, repeated.** Their false-positive rate mostly says which of the four fall above
  the threshold. It is not a rate over a population of unusual requests.
- **The t-interval** assumes roughly normal per-seed values. With 20 seeds this is reasonable, but
  not near 0% or 100%, where the interval is clipped.
- **Many tests.** Only the McNemar results with p < 0.0028 survive a Bonferroni correction. In Table
  4 every row with p < 0.001 does; the two rows with p = 1.000 are not differences at all, since
  there the two detectors decide in the same way on every request.

## 7. Reproducing the numbers

```bash
git checkout ca7de71
npm ci
npm run experiments          # about 1.5 minutes; writes results/<date>-<commit>/report.md
npm run report -- --update   # the same run, saved in numbers.json, and this chapter rewritten
```

The same seed always gives the same data, model, thresholds and bootstrap resamples. `results.json`
holds every seed, with its own Wilson and bootstrap intervals. The dashboard's _Detection quality_
page shows one seed live: ROC, confusion matrix, variants, McNemar.
